newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Imran says political foes trying to smear name.
newsitem.headline: Imran says political foes trying to smear name.

text.p: Former cricket star Imran Khan, bidding to clean up Pakistani politics, is facing what he calls a campaign to besmirch his name ahead of February 3 elections.

An ex-girlfriend, Sita White, has emerged from his playboy past saying that he is the father of her four-year-old daughter. Reports that she had filed a paternity suit in a Los Angeles court on Monday have made headlines in the local press.
"I have no comment," Imran told a news conference in the southern city of Karachi on Wednesday. "If we receive any court notice, then we will reply through our lawyer."
Under Pakistan's strict Islamic code, sex outside marriage is punishable by stoning to death, although the penalty has never been officially enforced.
On Tuesday Imran's Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) party said the affair was part of "a smear campaign sponsored by Imran Khan's political opponents to damage him".
It said two foreign newspapers had retracted stories alleging that Imran's party had received funds from his wealthy father-in-law Sir James Goldsmith, who is Jewish.
Some of Imran's Islamist opponents in Pakistan have accused him of taking money from Zionist interests.
"I haven't received a single paisa (one-hundredth of a rupee) from the Jewish lobby," he said in Karachi. "If anyone can prove it, I will leave politics and may be sent to jail."

Tehrik-i-Insaaf said Imran was the victim of a propaganda war to "divert the voter's attention from the real issues of loot, plunder and abuse by the professional politicians of Pakistan", adding that the campaign would backfire.
Imran, 44, launched his party only in April last year to crusade against corruption and stand up to foreign interests.

He has had little time to build a political machine to match those of his heavyweight rivals, Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) and the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) of Nawaz Sharif, which have long dominated politics.

But after President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, Imran decided to plunge his untested party into the elections being organised by a caretaker government.
"It is time for fresh faces to come into Pakistan's politics," he said at the time. "The people of Pakistan are fed up with the same faces and corrupt money."
Tehrik-i-Insaaf is not fielding candidates for all the seats in the 217-member National Assembly (lower house) and Imran himself is contesting nine, as allowed under electoral rules.
"This shows that he is not sure how many seats his party will get," said Islamabad-based journalist Zafar Abbas. "He is attracting large crowds, but he does not have a party."

Political analysts say Imran may take votes from the big parties, particularly the PML, and possibly affect the outcome of close contests between the two giants, but few believe his party will win more than a handful of seats.

Photogenic and admired for leading Pakistan to victory in the 1992 World Cup, Imran is respected for his achievement in raising funds to build a cancer hospital in the provincial capital Lahore, and appeals largely to the urban middle class.
Ahmed Rashid, a Lahore-based journalist, said the Sita White affair and other allegations could dent Imran's image for young people attracted by his stress on Islam and national pride.
"Lots of questions are going to be asked at his rallies and he will find campaigning difficult," Rashid said.

Both the PML and the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party, which is boycotting the elections on the grounds that an anti-corruption drive should be completed first, have begun to attack Imran over the accusations swirling around him.
Regardless of Imran's impact in the forthcoming polls, he can claim some credit for changing Pakistan's political agenda to focus on corruption and nepotism in high places.
"He is articulating widespread public scepticism about the political leadership and doing it very well," said Rashid.
